transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-01
Start time: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Arjun (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood CSM), Elena (CTO, Silverline), Ben (Lead ML Eng), Marta (SRE), Owen (Product)

Summary: Quick discovery focused on p95 latency targets, concurrency, streaming vs non-streaming behavior, and a tokens/sec benchmarking approach for Silverline's payment fraud real-time scorer. Customer evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC) options; primary constraints are p95 <= 250ms for short responses, concurrency ~200 parallel streams at peak, and streaming token-by-token output for client UX. Security / SOC2 / KMS questions were surfaced.

00:00:00 Jordan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick intro — I'm Jordan Hayes, AE at Redwood. With me is Maya and Arjun from SE, Priya from CS. Could you do quick intros on your side?
00:00:13 Elena (CTO): Hi — Elena Ruiz, CTO at Silverline, we run the payments infra and ML infra. Ben is our ML eng working on the fraud model. Marta does SRE and infra. Owen product.
00:00:25 Ben (Lead ML Eng): Hey all.
00:00:28 Maya (SE): Great. Goal for today is to understand your latency/throughput SLOs, concurrency and streaming needs so we can map to Hosted vs Dedicated or Private.

00:01:05 Owen (Product): To be explicit — we have a user-facing fraud score that needs to appear in the checkout flow in under, ideally, 200-250ms p95 for short contexts (~64 tokens). That is the hard requirement. We do have some background scoring that can be a bit slower.
00:01:30 Marta (SRE): On concurrency — during peak we see ~180-220 parallel requests to the scorer, each should stream partial output asap. We care a lot about cold-start and steady-state p95 behavior.
00:01:45 Jordan: Thanks. Can you describe current infra? Are you using in-house GPUs or cloud endpoints?
00:01:52 Elena: We're mostly on AWS today. We have some spot GPU workers running an internal LLaMa variant for offline and a tiny CPU service for quick heuristics in prod. But latency and scalability are pain points; batch jobs are fine but real-time is not.
00:02:12 Ben: We also have tokenizer differences — some prompts can be 40-80 tokens and others up to 1k for deeper analysis. For the checkout flow it's short.

00:02:40 Maya: Understood. For short sequences the model selection and serving mode matter a lot. Quick note: our Hosted API gives fastest time-to-value but it's multi-tenant; Dedicated gives predictable throughput (you reserve GPU pools) and Private/VPC gives the most isolation and KMS options.
00:03:05 Arjun (SE): Also FYI we have continuous batching, KV cache, and automatic prefix caching which helps warm workloads hit very low p95s; but cold-start and VM spin-up behavior will differ by deployment mode.

00:03:37 Ben: Can you share ballpark numbers — e.g., tokens per second, p95 for a 64-token prompt on Hosted vs Dedicated?
00:03:45 Maya: Sure — rough ballpark: on a modern 8xA100 or similar pool for a mid-size 13B-ish model, steady-state token throughput can be 2k-4k tokens/sec per GPU depending on quantization; p95 for 64-token short response in a well-warm setup can be sub-200ms on Dedicated with proper batching. Hosted may show slightly higher variance but similar medians. Bigger models (70B) will be higher latency.
00:04:20 Elena: The 200ms p95 is tight — does that assume streaming? We need the UX to show partial decisions within 150ms ideally.
00:04:30 Arjun: Streaming adds overhead per-token but reduces time-to-first-byte; it's often the best UX for partial results. For per-decision latency we tune chunk sizes and use prefix caching to minimize the first-token generation time. For 64 tokens we can often get first token under 120-150ms in Dedicated for smaller models.

00:05:05 Marta: How do you ensure p95 at scale — what about concurrency across many customers? We want predictable isolation so noisy neighbors don't kill us.
00:05:15 Maya: That is exactly where Dedicated helps — isolated GPU pools and configurable autoscaling. We can reserve capacity sized for your 220 concurrent steady sessions and provide burst capacity. We also offer routing policies to route critical traffic to higher tiers.

00:05:45 Ben: What about batching — doesn't batching increase latency for single requests if you wait to fill batches?
00:05:50 Arjun: Yes batching is a tradeoff. Our runtime uses workload-aware batching with latency SLOs per route. For critical checkout scorer routes we can set batch windows to micro-batching (few ms) or even disable batching in favor of immediate scheduling to meet p95. That reduces GPU efficiency but meets latency. We can show cost impact in the benchmark.

00:06:35 Owen: Tokens/sec numbers are helpful — can you give a practical benchmark plan so we can compare Hosted vs Dedicated vs our in-house?
00:06:45 Maya: We'll run a tokens/sec and p95 sweep: provide sample prompts and a traffic profile, we run against a pinned model variant (e.g., Llama-2-13B-quant) on Dedicated pool with and without streaming, and on Hosted equivalent. We'll report p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and cost per 1M tokens for each config.

00:07:12 Elena: Are there known gotchas with streaming and p95 calculations — e.g., network latency or client rendering time?
00:07:20 Arjun: Yes network RTT matters; our measurements typically isolate server-side latency (time-to-first-byte) and end-to-end (including network). We'll supply both numbers. For client rendering we'll instrument small JS example.

00:07:48 Ben: For our fraud scorer we also need deterministic outputs and version pinning — can you pin models and handle rollbacks?
00:07:55 Maya: Absolutely — model pinning, rollouts, and automatic fallback to smaller variants are all part of the platform. You can pin a model version per route and use canary rollouts.

00:08:20 Marta: Security: SOC2, encryption-at-rest, KMS integration — we need support for customer-managed keys, audit logs, and SSO/SAML for the console. Any limitations on Private?
00:08:32 Jordan: We do SOC2, support KMS/HSM integrations in Private and Dedicated via VPC options, and provide audit logs and RBAC. For Private we can also offer an on-prem package if needed; that gives you full control over the key lifecycle.

00:08:58 Elena: Good. Also compliance with PCI is a hard constraint — we can't send raw payment card data to third-party hosts. We will likely tokenize and send only hashed/non-sensitive fields, but we need confirm on data residency and encryption options.
00:09:15 Priya (CSM): We can share our security pack and past PCI notes — won't be perfect legal advice but it'll show what we support and previous customers.

00:09:30 Owen: Back to latency — explain cold vs warm p95. If a pod scales up, what's the cold p95 and how long to warm KV cache?
00:09:40 Arjun: Cold p95 includes container startup and model load, which can be seconds for big models (tens of seconds) if the instance isn't already provisioned. For Dedicated we recommend keeping a warm pool for critical routes. KV cache warming is near-instant for repeated prefixes; but the first request that triggers full model load will pay the spin-up tax. We can provide warm-start strategies and pre-warm hooks.

00:10:20 Ben: For tokens/sec benchmarking — do you allow us to run our harness in your environment or do you provide a harness we can run?
00:10:28 Maya: We provide a benchmark harness and can also accept your harness. For fairness we can run both. Our harness will report tokens/sec, latency distributions, GPU utilization, and token generation rates (tokens/sec per GPU). We usually run steady-state 10-minute runs and short-burst tests to emulate real checkout spikes.

00:10:55 Elena: Any special notes about seq length — some of our deep analysis has 1k tokens which is costly. For the checkout flow it's 64 tokens — so we care mostly about per-token overhead and model context window.
00:11:05 Arjun: Right. Larger seq lengths raise KV cache pressure and increase per-request compute; we'll test with your two representative seq lengths.

00:11:25 Ben: Do you support quantized model variants? That would help tokens/sec and cost.
00:11:30 Maya: Yes. We support various quantization profiles and will recommend profiles based on your latency and quality tradeoffs. For many workloads int8-like quantization gives 2-3x token throughput improvement with minor quality changes.

00:11:55 Marta: What about multi-tenant noise — if another tenant bursts, will it affect our Dedicated pool?
00:12:00 Jordan: Dedicated pools are isolated; noisy neighbor risk is minimal. Hosted is multi-tenant, but we do capacity caps and prioritization policies. For strict isolation choose Dedicated or Private.

00:12:25 Owen: Let's talk numbers. If we need p95 <= 250ms for 64-token responses, and concurrency 220, what's the ballpark infra?
00:12:34 Arjun: Very rough: if you disable large batching and aim for micro-batching, you need enough GPUs so steady-state per-GPU throughput can handle the token RPS. Example: assume each request returns ~64 tokens -> ~64 * 220 = 14k tokens per second sustained. If a single GPU at your chosen quantized model can do ~3k tokens/sec steady, you'd need 5 GPUs reserved to meet throughput (14k/3k ~4.7), plus buffer for bursts, so 6-8 GPUs in Dedicated pool. That assumes warm caches and efficient scheduling.
00:13:12 Ben: That helps — also cost implications?
00:13:15 Jordan: We'll provide a cost model after we know model size and exact quantization. But expect Dedicated monthly commit pricing; Hosted is pay-as-you-go and easier to start.

00:13:40 Elena: For the POC we want: 1) baseline tokens/sec and p95 on your Hosted; 2) Dedicated run with reserved GPUs matching our concurrency; 3) compare vs our in-house nodes. Can Redwood run the POC with the real sample traffic?
00:13:55 Maya: Yes — if you provide a corpus and traffic profile we can run it in a test isolate. We prefer to pin model variant and quantization to avoid noisy comparison.

00:14:20 Owen: About streaming — we need partial results to begin rendering in the UI within 120ms ideally. Is that realistic?
00:14:28 Arjun: For very small prompts yes on Dedicated with warm caches we can get first token under 120ms. We will show time-to-first-byte and time-to-last-byte. If network RTT is small this is realistic.

00:14:55 Ben: Are there SDKs for streaming and client retries?
00:15:00 Maya: Yes SDKs in JS/Python and websocket/HTTP streaming. We also provide server-side retries and automatic fallback to smaller models for availability.

00:15:25 Marta: Any constraints with VPC/private on streaming?
00:15:30 Jordan: No functional constraints, though setup requires additional networking work; Private gives you more control but takes longer to provision.

00:16:05 Elena: What about RBAC and access in Dedicated — can we restrict who can deploy model rollouts?
00:16:12 Priya: Yes RBAC, SSO/SAML, audit logs, and route-level permissioning. We can map to your IAM.

00:16:40 Ben: For the benchmark harness we'll provide one endpoint that simulates checkout — 40-80 token prompts with structured fields. Also a longer analysis endpoint at 1k tokens. We'll want separate p95 targets: 250ms for checkout, 2s for analysis.
00:16:58 Maya: Perfect. We'll run both. We'll also show per-token cost and GPU util.

00:17:20 Owen: Can you scope a quick math for pricing per-month if we reserve 8 GPUs?
00:17:27 Jordan: I'll send a dedicated pricing sheet with commit tiers, burst pricing and estimated token costs after we pick model. Expect a mix of fixed reserved cost + variable token usage.

00:17:45 Ben: Any internal tooling for tracing per-request token cost?
00:17:50 Arjun: Console has token-level cost breakdown, per-route latency breakdown and tracing hooks you can push into your APM.

00:18:12 Elena: Are there any latency percentiles we should watch in production beyond p95?
00:18:17 Maya: p99 is also critical for UX; we'll provide p50/p95/p99. p99 may spike due to occasional GC or cold starts; we recommend alerts on p95 and p99.

00:18:40 Marta: Regarding logs — can we retain request-level logs for 90 days and tie them to our audit system?
00:18:46 Jordan: Yes, we offer configurable retention; longer retention is an add-on and we can stream logs to your S3 or SIEM.

00:19:05 Ben: Any examples of customers with similar latency constraints in payments?
00:19:10 Jordan: We have a few payment and fintech customers — we can connect you to anonymized case studies and share a benchmark spreadsheet.

00:19:30 Elena: Ok let's talk blockers — timeline wise we want to run a POC and decide by end of April. Security review needs to be done in parallel.
00:19:40 Jordan: That's doable. We'll target POC week of Apr 13, security pack early next week.

00:19:58 Owen: Do you have SLA numbers for Dedicated?
00:20:02 Jordan: Yes Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; we'll include the SLA doc in the pack.

00:20:15 Ben: Technical deep dive question — how do you handle KV cache eviction when many prefixes are unique (our telemetry IDs)?
00:20:22 Arjun: If prefix uniqueness is high cache hit will be low; we recommend deterministic prefixing (strip ids) or server-side prefix normalization to increase cache hits. We'll show caching impact during the benchmark.

00:20:45 Marta: What's the overhead of quantization on quality? We need to verify fraud model classifier fidelity.
00:20:52 Maya: We'll do quality checks: you provide a labeled eval set and we run regressions comparing reference model vs quantized variant. If accuracy drops beyond threshold we recommend different tradeoffs.

00:21:20 Elena: Ok let's recap next steps verbally.
00:21:25 Jordan: Recap: Redwood will share pricing, security docs (SOC2, KMS options), and benchmark harness. Silverline to provide prompts, sample traffic profiles, and security contact. We'll schedule a POC the week of Apr 13.
00:21:40 Ben: Sounds good.
00:21:42 Marta: I'll send security contact details to Jordan.
00:21:46 Jordan: Great. Anything else?
00:21:50 Owen: No, thanks.
00:21:52 Jordan: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts.

00:22:10 [call continues — more informal notes and small clarifications, some crosstalk]
00:25:00 Elena: Minor note — our product sometimes does synchronous and async; we may want hybrid routing where checkout is synchronous on dedicated pool and batched async on cheaper nodes.
00:25:25 Maya: We support routing policies and automatic fallback; can configure per-route behavior.
00:26:10 Ben: We'll also include error injection tests in the POC.
00:26:25 Arjun: Good idea — we'll add resilience tests to the harness.
00:27:00 [transcription noise: "KV cash" appears a few times instead of "KV cache"]
00:29:30 Owen: On the SDK side we want retry semantics documented — default retries, idempotency concerns.
00:29:40 Priya: We'll include SDK docs and recommended retry patterns.
00:31:12 Elena: If Dedicated is the right call, is there a minimum commit?
00:31:20 Jordan: Yes minimum commit depends on region and GPU type — I'll include exact numbers in the pricing sheet.
00:33:00 Ben: For the tokens/sec metric, will you provide GPU-level telemetry?
00:33:06 Arjun: Yes GPU util, power draw, and tokens/sec per GPU are in the benchmark report.
00:35:05 Marta: We care about metrics being reproducible. Can we re-run tests?
00:35:12 Maya: Yes we'll provide the harness and logs so you can re-run. We'll also provide configuration to pin randomness seeds for deterministic runs where applicable.
00:37:00 [wrap-up small talk] 
00:50:00 Jordan: Thanks everyone. Follow-ups to come.
